title: Code of Conduct
text: Imageomics Code of Conduct As members of the Imageomics community, we agree to maintain an environment where every person feels welcome to be their true self and speak from the heart. As such, all members of the Imageomics Institute community agree to abide by the principles outlined in our Code of Conduct. Imageomics Code of Conduct We agree as individuals and as a group to: Listen to understand. When one person talks, others listen. Speak to be understood. We use lay terms and are patient with people who are not experts in our specific field. We are all learning, no matter who we are. Embrace “Yes and...” Focus on possibilities instead of obstacles. Embrace others' ideas and honor divergence of thought. Take space / make space. Those who tend to talk a lot are intentional about letting others talk first, while those who tend to hold back are intentional about contributing. Beware of blind spots. We do not know what we do not know. We are vigilant for differences among our experiences and positions. Respect time. Once a meeting or session time concludes, we need to move on. Be proactive in scheduling time for follow-up and ongoing in-depth conversations. Care for each other. We bring our full selves to the community, and we look out for each other wholeheartedly. AI Use Policy Borrowed from CRA . Allowable use of AI tools that do not share or use the data for training. Requires permission if recording others. Language to use when requesting permission: “We would like to use during this discussion to assist with note-taking. records and transcribes audio and can produce a summary of the discussion. The audio and transcription will only be saved and used internally. Please let us know if you object to the use of .” Scope We abide by these principles in all Imageomics spaces, including but not limited to digital and in-person meetings, formal and informal gatherings, online discussion forums and chat spaces, and field and lab work. Acts of misconduct are prohibited. Those found to engage in misconduct will be subject to dismissal from the project and further actions as directed by the guidelines of the employers, federal law, and the place of incidence. Reporting Misconduct If you believe you have experienced or witnessed misconduct in an Imageomics setting, please take these steps: Document the incident. Tell someone you trust. Report the incident to Diane or Tanya. Privacy will be protected to the greatest extent possible.

title: Community Values
text: Community Values Transparency We ensure our efforts are clear about assumptions, uncertainty, and limits, and provide open sources of information, processes, and discovery. Accountability We are responsible, individually and collectively, for the outcomes we produce and ensure, to the best of our abilities, that the methods outcome matches intended use. Collaboration We create and nurture collaborative environments and welcome, value, and affirm all members of our community. We also consider how and for whom solutions are created and promote the heterogeneity of perspectives in the creation process. We actively engage others' perspectives, recognize everyone's potential to contribute new ideas, and work together to find creative solutions to complex problems. Safety We ensure our practices are ethical and impartial to the best of our ability. We address ethical issues when we discover them and practice good data governance. We strive to enhance practices while openly addressing those that harm people or the environment. View the Imageomics Code of Conduct

title: The Vision of the Imageomics Institute
text: The Vision of the Imageomics Institute Imageomics establishes a new scientific field that uses biological images, data science, computing, and machine learning to accelerate discovery across the living world. About the Imageomics Institute NSF OAC-2118240 Mission Creating a collaborative research, training, and community-facing environment for extracting existing and new biological traits from images of organisms, with the necessary infrastructure for cyber, information, and model development. The Institute will advance Imageomics-enabled biology, accelerate innovations in machine learning, and create digital resources for researchers and practitioners in biology, data science, and machine learning, as well as the broader scientific community. It will further interdisciplinary training and education, and engage the broader public in the scientific process. Accomplishing these tasks will provide unique insights and enable biological discovery over a wide range of informative organismal attributes, some not yet comprehended or studied, and across multiple scales of biological organization from individuals to species. Vision To establish a new scientific field called imageomics that harnesses revolutions in data science and computing, as well as the rapidly expanding collections of biological image data, in order to accelerate biological understanding of phenotypic traits extracted from images of organisms. The Imageomics Institute will make the study of the interrelationships, associations, and dynamics of traits computable by using the existing structured biological knowledge to inform the computational methods. It will develop integrated, interdisciplinary approaches to advance the state of the art in knowledge-guided machine learning while rapidly accelerating biological discovery and public engagement in science, forming a virtuous cycle. Contributions Digital resources for the scientific community and practitioners in biology, data science, and machine learning. Advancements in Imageomics-enabled biology. Innovations in machine learning. Advancements in interdisciplinary training and education. Engagement of the broader public in the scientific process by leveraging images as the source of data to democratize science. imageomics | brand-new noun i-'mi-jə-'ō-miks A new scientific field in which computational machine learning tools built around biological knowledge bases are used by biologists to analyze image data in order to characterize patterns and gain insights into traits and relationships at individual, population and species scales, insights that then get incorporated into the algorithms that run the tools. Imageomics Institute | brand-new entity 'i-mi-jə-'ō-miks 'in(t)-stə-tÜt The NSF Harnessing the Data Revolution institute (NSF OAC-2118240) established October 1, 2021, to create machine learning tools using publicly funded collections of digital image data from national centers, field stations, museums and individual laboratories that will enable scientists to study how function follows form in all areas of biology and expand public understanding of the rules of Life on Earth and how it evolves. See also: One of five inaugural institutes for data-intensive research in science and engineering established by the NSF. Technical Abstract The traits that characterize living organisms, in particular their morphology, physiology, behavior and genetic make-up, enable them to cope with forces of the physical as well as the biological and social environments that impinge on them. Moreover, since function follows form, traits provide the raw material upon which natural selection operates, thus shaping evolutionary trajectories and the history of life. Interestingly, most living organisms, from microscopic microbes to charismatic megafauna, reveal themselves visually and are routinely captured in copious images taken by humans from all walks of life. The resulting massive amount of image data has the potential to further our understanding of how multifaceted traits of organisms shape the behavior of individuals, collectives, populations, and the ecological communities they live in, as well as the evolutionary trajectories of the species they comprise. Images are increasingly the currency for documenting the details of life on the planet, and yet traits of organisms, known or novel, cannot be readily extracted from them. Just like with genomic data two decades ago, our ability to collect data at the moment far outstrips our ability to extract biological insight from it. The Institute will establish a new field of Imageomics, in which biologists utilize machine learning algorithms to analyze vast stores of existing image data, especially publicly funded digital collections from national centers, field stations, museums and individual laboratories, to characterize patterns and gain novel insights on how function follows form in all areas of biology to expand our understanding of the rules of life on Earth and how it evolves. This Institute will introduce structured knowledge from the biological sciences to guide and structure machine learning algorithms to enable biological trait discovery from images, establishing the field of Imageomics. With images captured and annotated by scientists and the public serving as the basis for the work, the Institute's convergent approach uses structured biological knowledge to provide scientifically validated inductive biases and rich supervision for machine learning, and machine learning will in turn enrich the body of biological knowledge. The resulting models and tools will help make what was hidden visible, so that scientists from a wide range of biological communities can discover and infer the traits of organisms; assess shared similarities and differences between individuals, populations and species; and come to see the world in new ways. Imageomics will accelerate and transform the biomedical, agricultural and basic biological sciences as they seek to understand and control genes that relate to particular phenotypes and enable an overarching understanding of how the genome evolved in tandem with the organismal phenome. Because traits are the essential links between genes and the environment, using machine learning to help characterize them will lead to emergent understandings of how they function. Harnessing the insights that arise from these new visualizations will stimulate the use of new genetic technologies, such as CRISPR, and more nuanced ecological practices, such as modified land use schemes that emerge from better understanding the connections between individual decision-making within species and their impact on their population dynamics. With the emergence of new and better targeted practices that generate fewer unintended consequences, the new linkages resulting from a better understanding of traits and their consequences will bolster the nation's bioeconomy. In addition, by leveraging and expanding existing diverse, inclusive and intellectually wide-ranging collaborative networks, the Institute will also educate the next generation of scientists and engage the broader public in scientific inquiry and knowledge discovery so that Imageomics can transform and democratize science for public good. The Vision of the Imageomics Institute

title: Visitors to Imageomics Institute
text: Visiting Traveler Instructions Please follow the procedures outlined below for travel funded by the Imageomics Institute. Failure to comply with these guidelines may result in the forfeiture of approved travel funding. Review the Ohio State Travel Policy before your departure. By accepting travel funds from the Imageomics Institute you are required to adhere to all federal and university policies. We recommend you review the OSU travel website for additional travel resources. Complete our traveler intake form to establish a payee profile in our accounting system. Following submission of the traveler intake form our travel coordinator will reach out to OSU's travel agency to book your airfare. Review the proposed itinerary , provide any frequent flyer account number and TSA PreCheck, if applicable. Once you approve the airfare , our travel coordinator will book it using a spend authorization (SA) number, and you will receive an email confirmation. Please note, any airfare must be on a U.S. carrier and in economy/coach to be reimbursed. Other travel expenses may be eligible for reimbursement, up to the maximum amount specified by the Imageomics Institute, only if they are pre-approved in advance. Please save your itemized receipts for all expenses. IMPORTANT: Within 30 days of your travel, you are required to send all itemized receipts directly to imageomics-contact@osu.edu .

title: Project Spotlight: Making Models and Mining Mimics
text: Project Spotlight: Making Models and Mining Mimics Event dates Mon, Nov 14 2022, 3 - 4pm Event link Join Zoom Meeting Event details A common point of contact between biology and computer science uses machine learning (ML) and computer vision to classify species. For example, iNaturalist, Merlin, Seek. Building upon previous work in this field, this talk will explore current work being done to expand ML algorithms to capture the biological mechanisms underlying Mullerian (where both species are chemically defended) mimicry in Heliconius butterflies. By modifying the training methods and inputs used in machine learning, computer vision is capable of asking biologically relevant questions. One approach, which modified the training method, trained classification on one Heliconius species before testing on its mimic, in order to approximate the training and learning process undertaken by avian predators. Another sought to account for the visual complexities of butterfly mimicry by adjusting the visual acuity of the images to better represent butterfly and bird vision. Finally, we quantified similarities and differences in the phenotypic spaces created by mimetic species. In the time remaining, I will talk about current work being done to identify traits and to perform genotype-phenotype analysis using Heliconius. title: ML & Biology Fastlane
text: ML & Biology Fastlane Event dates Mon, Dec 5 2022, 3 - 4pm Event link Join Zoom Meeting Event details We present a simple method for improving large vision model performance on multiple downstream tasks. The current trend of research is to remove as much inductive bias as possible from model architectures and let them learn patterns from the data. We instead add inductive bias to the pre-training objective, rather than the model, in the form of domain-specific knowledge. Because we introduce inductive bias as a simple pre-training objective, the pre-trained weights are extremely flexible and can be easily applied to many tasks with no additional modification. We show that knowledge-guided pre-training improves pre-training convergence and downstream performance in many tasks and data distributions, especially in data-scarce regimes. title: External Speaker Series: Biodiversity across space and time: Insights from trait-based ecology
text: External Speaker Series: Biodiversity across space and time: Insights from trait-based ecology Event dates Mon, May 15 2023, 3 - 4pm Registration Register Event details Marta Jarzyna, Assistant Professor, Evolution, Ecology and Organismal Biology, The Ohio State Trait-based ecology has recently been heralded as the key to pinpointing relevant mechanisms and thus making generalizable ecological predictions. To date, however, lack of knowledge regarding the responses of specific organismal traits to environmental changes across spatiotemporal scales has hindered efforts to make trait-based ecology a predictive science. In my talk, I will discuss how expansive and growing repositories of species traits and their geographic distributions, often replicated across time, can help shed light on mechanisms underlying biodiversity dynamics across varied spatial and temporal scales. Bio: Marta Jarzyna is an Assistant Professor in the Department of Evolution, Ecology and Organismal Biology at The Ohio State University. She is a broad-scale ecologist and global change biologist interested in understanding the processes underlying biodiversity dynamics across different spatial, temporal, and taxonomic scales. smiling woman with blue eyes and brown hair stands in front of a book case External Speaker Series: Biodiversity across space and time: Insights from trait-based ecology Mon, May 15 2023 2023-05-15 Marta Jarzyna, Assistant Professor, Evolution, Ecology and Organismal Biology... smiling woman with blue eyes and brown hair stands in front of a book case

title: Imageomics Research Forum featuring Andrew Senin, Drexel University
text: Imageomics Research Forum featuring Andrew Senin, Drexel University Event dates Mon, May 1 2023, 3 - 4pm Event link Join Zoom Meeting Event details This month’s research forum will feature the work of Andrew Senin of Drexel University. Andrew Senin, a computer science major at Drexel University has been working under Dr. David Breen's and Dr. Jane Greenburg's guidance, with input from Tulane colleagues on automatic fish outlining and analysis as part of his senior design research project. Please join us as Andrew shares his research on Fourier descriptors as shape features for object (e.g. fish specimen) outlines. Abstract: Outlines are a fundamental object of study in any morphometric analysis of biological specimens. They help answer scientific questions about a species' behavior, geography, and evolution. Online specimen image collections are a rich source of outlines, best used by extracting outlines via automated methods. But automated methods must account for significant variation in image quality and configuration, and represent extracted outlines in a way that facilitates answering the scientific question at hand. Our ongoing work extracts outlines from a subset of specimens in the INHS Fish Collection and explores what scientific questions they can answer with an elliptical Fourier analysis. Representing specimens' outlines by their elliptic Fourier descriptors, we've trained machine learning models to infer a specimen's species from its outline and identify distinguishing features of each species' outlines. Elliptic Fourier analysis also enables the visualizations of a species' average shape as well as cross-shapes between two or more specimens. title: Imageomics Research Forum: Querying the Real World: Data Exploration in Augmented Reality
text: Imageomics Research Forum: Querying the Real World: Data Exploration in Augmented Reality Event dates Mon, Jun 12 2023, 3 - 4pm Event link Join Zoom Event Event details Arnab Nandi, Associate Professor of Computer Science & Engineering at The Ohio State University. There is a vast amount of structured data present in real-world objects and scenarios such as movie posters, airport displays, and grocery aisles. Given recent advances in computer vision and cloud-based data infrastructure, we are faced with a new opportunity to enable interactive exploration of real-world data using augmented reality. In this talk, we will first look at ARQuery, an interface that uses augmented reality to enable ad-hoc querying over the real world. Using an interaction and visualization grammar designed specifically to interactively explore real-world data, ARQuery provides a fluid experience that is significantly faster and easier-to-use than traditional approaches. Second, we discuss Quill, a domain-specific language for developing data-intensive augmented reality applications. We demonstrate how Quill can expedite and democratize an otherwise complex development process. In addition to reducing programming effort, we show that Quill-generated applications can automatically include optimizations, allowing them to be more performant than applications that are not built with Quill. Bio: Arnab Nandi is an Associate Professor of Computer Science & Engineering at The Ohio State University. Arnab's work focuses on bridging data infrastructure with human interaction, spanning areas of database systems, human factors, and next-generation interfaces. Arnab is a recipient of the US National Science Foundation's CAREER Award, IEEE's TCDE Early Career Award for his contributions towards user-focused data interaction, The Ohio State University's Alumni Award for Distinguished Teaching, and the University's Early Career Innovator of the Year Award. At Ohio State, he co-founded the OHI/O Program, that fosters a tech culture through hackathons and informal learning, and The STEAM Factory, an interdisciplinary research and collaboration network. Most recently, Arnab served as Vice President of Data Science at Azuga Inc. (a Bridgestone company) after the acquisition of his connected vehicles analytics startup, Mobikit. title: Imageomics Speaker Series: AIs in the Forest: Towards Computational Field Biology
text: Imageomics Speaker Series: AIs in the Forest: Towards Computational Field Biology Event dates Mon, Jun 5 2023, 3 - 4pm Event link Join Talk Event details Tilo Burghardt, UG Programme Director at the Dept of Computer Science at Bristol University, UK. In 1963, the British conservationist Sir Peter Scott and his family started re-identifying individual Bewick's swans from hand drawings of unique beak patterns during the species' annual migratory visit to the Slimbridge wetlands near Bristol. This study still runs today and represents one of the earliest and longest standing individual animal identification projects in the world. Over the last 60 years digital technology, communication networks, and now artificial intelligence have transformed such gathering and interpretation of ecologically relevant data for field biology and firmly placed measuring manifestations of life (i.e. bio-metrics) in the computational realm. This talk will trace some of the key concepts at the heart of this evolving subject cluster - from earliest ideas to current AI-driven systems. It will try to relate emerging modern terminology such as imageomics, animal biometrics, and ecological computer science within the wider context of computation and biology. Finally, the talk will try to depict examples how today's 'third revolution' in visual computational biology is being applied to conservation, ecology, and even farming, and how neighbouring disciplines such as robotics, genetics, remote sensing, behavioural sciences, and taxonomics can contribute towards evolving the subject. Various lines of work at the University of Bristol will serve as examples to show the diversity of the emerging interdisciplinary science. The talk will highlight some key technical challenges today and call for a renewed focus on cross-disciplinary science. Bio: Dr. Tilo Burghardt is a computer science academic who researches animal biometrics and computer vision methods for the life sciences. His work focuses on using artificial intelligence and robotics to support biodiversity, sustainability, and animal welfare. His interdisciplinary research links computing with ecology, conservation, taxonomics, healthcare, animal husbandry, and sustainable farming. He was one of the first researchers to monitor animals in their natural habitat via automated real-time computer vision methods in the early 2000s. Over the past two decades he made contributions to establishing animal biometrics as an emerging cross-discipline linked to imageomics and routed in pattern recognition and artificial intelligence. Tilo's enthusiasm for computer science and computer vision is reflected in his dedication to teaching the subject. He has received the University of Bristol 'Award for Education' for his educational contributions to the Engineering Faculty. close up photo of a man with blond hair, beard and mustache and blue eyes. title: QUEST Teacher Training Program
text: QUEST Teacher Training Program Event dates Mon, Oct 9 2023, 4 - 5pm Event link Register for Zoom Meeting Event details At this month's Imageomics Research Forum, Dan Rubenstein and Leanna House will provide a recap of this past summer's QUEST Teacher Preparation Program . This summer the program featured In Our Back Yards: Human Impacts on Pollinator and Plant Populations in Local Environments. During QUEST, local educators posed questions of their own making about the ways humans impact pollinators in local environments. They were able to explore varied human impacts that range from taming wild lands to domesticated properties to the styles of farming that produce our food (organic vs. conventional). In this mini-research experience, educators ventured outdoors to take pictures of plants and the insects that use them. They then used images that characterize wild and domesticated habitats in terms of their diversity, distribution, size and connectivity in order to test hypotheses they generated about how such landscape features and other human impacts affect pollinators and the plants they rely on for survival and reproduction. By collaborating with peer educators, teachers model the interactions that their students will use when engaging in their own experiential learning activities during the school year. QUEST encourages educators to let their sense of wonder lead as they explore the process of scientific inquiry through images. title: Imageomics Speaker Series: Janna Hastings, University of Zurich
text: Imageomics Speaker Series: Janna Hastings, University of Zurich Event dates Mon, Nov 20 2023, 4 - 5pm Event link Register for Zoom Meeting Event details Ontology pre-training as a strategy to improve data-driven predictions: Recent breakthroughs in artificial intelligence have resulted from the combination of big data with large-scale neural networks. However, neural networks face several challenges: they are opaque and cannot offer explanations, they are vulnerable to adversarial challenges, they can be brittle and lack generalisability, and their operation cannot be controlled in semantic terms accessible to domain experts. With an application to prediction of chemical properties from chemical structures, I will describe an approach to enhance the training of neural network-based predictive systems with ontology pre-training. With this strategy, the meaningful classifications from a domain ontology are taught to the network first in a dedicated training phase before the network is fine-tuned for the specific property prediction task. We have been able to show that this strategy improves prediction performance, reduces training time and improves the interpretability of the associated model. Speaker Bio: Janna Hastings was born in Cape Town, South Africa where she completed her undergraduate studies in Mathematics and Computer Science. Thereafter, she moved to Cambridge, UK to join the Cheminformatics and Metabolism group at the European Bioinformatics Institute (2006-2015) where she led the development of the ChEBI molecular ontology and metabolism knowledgebase. She completed part-time Master's degrees in Computer Science (University of South Africa, 2011) and Philosophy (Open University, 2012). She obtained her PhD in Computational Biology from the University of Cambridge (2015-2019), where she studied the role of metabolism in healthy ageing using multi-omics data and a time-series modelling approach. She completed postdoctoral studies at the Otto-von-Guericke University Magdeburg (2019-2022) working at the intersection between knowledge-based systems and artificial intelligence, at the EPFL (2020-2022) in neurodegenerative disease bioinformatics, and with the Human Behaviour-Change Project at University College London (2017-2022) where she helped to create an artificial intelligence-driven knowledge system for evidence about human behavior change to support decision-making, policy and practice. Since August 2022 she has been an Assistant Professor of Medical Knowledge and Decision Support at the Institute for Implementation Science in Health Care, Faculty of Medicine, University of Zurich, and Vice-Director of the School of Medicine at the University of St. Gallen. The focus of her research is on digitalization in the clinic and how new digital technologies can be harnessed to accelerate biomedical discovery and improve the working lives of clinicians. smiling woman with blue eyes and light skin. title: External Speaker Series: Justin Kitzes on Automated Acoustics Surveys for Understanding and Predicting Biodiversity at Scale
text: External Speaker Series: Justin Kitzes on Automated Acoustics Surveys for Understanding and Predicting Biodiversity at Scale Event dates Mon, Jan 29 2024, 4 - 5pm Event link Register for Zoom Meeting Event details Abstract: The availability of accurate, large-scale, long-term data on species diversity and abundance form a critical foundation for understanding, predicting, and ultimately prevent biodiversity loss. In this talk, I will discuss new developments in the field of bioacoustics that are allowing ecologists to gather and analyze data on terrestrial wildlife at increasingly large spatiotemporal scales. First, I will describe our approach to combining inexpensive field sensors, machine learning, and statistical models for surveying songbirds, frogs, and other taxa in the field. Second, I will describe how we have used this framework to draw new insights across the fields of natural history, conservation, and ecology. Speaker Bio: Justin Kitzes is an Assistant Professor of Biological Sciences at the University of Pittsburgh. His research broadly examines how species are distributed across complex landscapes, and how human impacts drive these distributions, with a particular focus on the ecology and conservation of rare and hard-to-detect species. To better study these species, his work relies heavily on techniques from terrestrial bioacoustics, specifically automated acoustic field recorders and machine learning models for sound detection and classification. His lab both develops methods and tools to enable bioacoustics research and applies these methods to answer questions spanning natural history, conservation, and ecology. title: External Speaker Series: Ulrik Pagh Schultz Lundquist on WildDrone – Autonomous Drones for Nature Conservation Missions
text: External Speaker Series: Ulrik Pagh Schultz Lundquist on WildDrone – Autonomous Drones for Nature Conservation Missions Event dates Mon, Feb 5 2024, 10 - 11am Event link Register for Zoom Meeting Event details Abstract: The WildDrone project aims to revolutionize wildlife conservation practices by using autonomous drone technology as a unifying platform to monitor wildlife populations, track their movements, and manage human-wildlife conflicts. The WildDrone consortium will train 13 doctoral candidates and equip them with a unique combination of multidisciplinary skills for drone-based ecology and wildlife conservation. The candidates will work closely together in a global training network to realize the full potential of drones and companion autonomous systems for nature conservation missions. In this talk I will give an overview of the WildDrone network, research and training activities, our interdisciplinary methodology, and the specific drone-related research currently taking place in the project. Speaker Bio: Ulrik Pagh Schultz Lundquist is Professor and Head of the Center for SDU UAS, the drone center at University of Southern Denmark. He is currently coordinator of the WildDrone Marie Curie Network and is interested in the design and implementation of aerial, mobile, and self-organizing robotic systems with a focus on the use of high-level software abstractions to achieve safety, reliability, and robustness. a heard of animals on the savannah is viewed from above as captured by a drone man with shaved head, black rimmed glasses with blue eyes, light skin, and a beard and mustache looks toward the camera. Imageomics aims to computationally analyze traits from images, covering morphology, physiology, behavior, and genetic characteristics of organisms. Our primary goal is to ensure that AI models are firmly grounded in established scientific knowledge, enabling them to provide predictions that are both broadly applicable and biologically relevant. The workshop's broader vision is to foster a community of researchers at the intersection of AI and biology, actively contributing to the development of the field of Imageomics, which is experiencing rapid growth. We invite experts and scholars from various fields to submit research papers exploring the applications of artificial intelligence and machine learning techniques for deciphering characteristic patterns within image and video data of organisms. text: Public Lecture: AI for Nature featuring Dr. Tanya Berger Wolf Event dates Mon, Oct 7 2024, 4 - 5pm Registration Register for Remote or In-person attendance Event link Public Lecture: AI for Nature Event details Please register to attend a Public Lecture hosted by the AI and Biodiversity Change Global Climate Center and the Montreal Botanical Gardens on Monday, October 7 at 4 PM ET (UTC-05:00), featuring speaker Dr. Tanya Berger-Wolf, Director of the Global Climate Center for AI and Biodiversity Change (ABC) , a multi-national center funded by the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada (NSERC) and United States National Science Foundation (NSF). Abstract Dr. Berger-Wolf explores how AI is transforming the study and our decisions about nature by turning vast new data sources, such as GPS, high-definition cameras, autonomous vehicles under water, on the ground, and in the air, genotyping, acoustic sensors, and crowdsourcing, into high resolution information source about living organisms, enabling scientific inquiry, conservation, and policy decisions. title: Seminar: Ofir Levy, School of Zoology at Tel Aviv University, presentation, "AI in Ecology: Refining Microclimate Predictions and Thermoregulatory Tracking"
text: Seminar: Ofir Levy, School of Zoology at Tel Aviv University, presentation, "AI in Ecology: Refining Microclimate Predictions and Thermoregulatory Tracking" Event dates Mon, Oct 28 2024, 4 - 5pm Registration Register here to attend Event details Who: Announcing the upcoming talk from Ofir Levy, School of Zoology at Tel Aviv University When: October 28 at 4pm ET Title: "AI in Ecology: Refining Microclimate Predictions and Thermoregulatory Tracking" Abstract: Climate conditions that animals experience are a major force determining their survival, life-history, activity patterns, and fitness. To calculate these forces and estimate the impacts of environmental change, we must deeply understand the microclimates they experience (i.e., climate conditions in their proximity) and how these conditions influence their lives. Traditional methods of measuring microclimates involve labor-intensive fieldwork, and existing microclimate models often need refinement to accurately capture the true conditions animals face. Traditional thermoregulation tracking methods can be observational or invasive, potentially disturbing natural behaviors. In the era of big data and AI advancements, we can enhance our understanding of microclimates and non-invasively monitor thermoregulatory behaviors. Using drone data and a spatial heat-balance microclimate model, we demonstrate that a random-forest model can predict and correct microclimate model errors, highlighting overlooked parameters in microclimate calculations. Additionally, we reveal behavioral thermoregulation patterns using camera-trap data combined with computer vision AI and microclimate measurements. This approach enables continuous tracking of animal microhabitat preferences under varying conditions. Our findings suggest that AI models can bolster our capacity to understand the thermal environment and animal behavior, thereby informing conservation strategies in our changing climate. Bio: Ofir Levy is a Senior Lecturer at the School of Zoology at Tel Aviv University since 2018. He earned his Ph.D. from Tel Aviv University's Department of Zoology in 2010, where his research focused on understanding how ecological, physiological, and evolutionary forces shape organismal activity patterns. Following this doctoral work, he completed a postdoctoral appointment at the School of Life Sciences at Arizona State University in 2017. He has utilized field studies and computer simulations ever since, to explore how habitat loss and climate change affect animal performance and survival. More recently, he expanded his research to include the use of artificial intelligence to gain a deeper understanding of the environment and animal responses to various climatic conditions. This includes developing AI-driven tools for identifying animals’ responses to climate through camera traps and creating high-resolution microclimate mapping to support biodiversity research and management. title: Imageomics Seminar: Dr. Maks Ovsjanikov, November 22, 2024
text: Imageomics Seminar: Dr. Maks Ovsjanikov, November 22, 2024 Event dates Fri, Nov 22 2024, 10 - 10:45am Registration Register here to attend Event details Imageomics Seminar: Dr. Maks Ovsjanikov, November 22, 2024 November 22, 2024, 10am ET Title: Novel 3D deep learning approaches for robust shape comparison and analysis Abstract: Recent years have witnessed several major advances in 3D data acquisition. However, techniques for processing and analyzing 3D data often lag behind their 2D counterparts. This is, in part, due to the challenges related to the lack of a canonical grid-like representation for 3D point clouds or surfaces, and, at the same time, the limited scope of data for training. In this talk, I will first describe a robust learning approach on curved surfaces using learned diffusion. I will then give several applications, including protein and RNA molecule analysis, cell tracking in 3D, and unsupervised representation learning via robust non-rigid 3D correspondence methods. Bio: Maks Ovsjanikov is a Professor at Ecole Polytechnique in France. He works on 3D shape analysis with emphasis on deep learning techniques for shape matching and correspondence. He has received a Eurographics Young Researcher Award, an ERC Starting Grant, a CNRS Bronze Medal (highest recognition for junior researchers in France), and an ERC Consolidator Grant in 2023. His works have received 11 best paper awards or nominations at top conferences, including CVPR, ICCV, 3DV, as well as a SIGGRAPH 2023 Test-of-time award. His main research topics include 3D shape comparison and deep learning on 3D data. title: FathomVerse: Explore the Depths
text: FathomVerse: Explore the Depths Event dates Mon, Feb 24 2025, 4 - 5pm Registration go.osu.edu/kakani-katija Event details Abstract: The deep sea is the largest habitable ecosystem on the planet and remains one of the least explored. Very little is known about deep sea inhabitants, their behavior, and the limits and drivers for their survival. Researchers estimate that anywhere between 30-60% of life in the ocean is unknown to science, and these gaps in knowledge need to be filled to inform exploitative activities like aquaculture, offshore wind, and deep-sea mining. In order to fully explore our ocean and effectively steward the life that lives there, we need to increase our capacity for biological observations; massive disparities in effort between visual data collection and annotation make it prohibitively challenging to process this information. State-of-the-art approaches in automation and machine learning cannot solve this problem alone, and we must aggressively build an integrated community of educators, taxonomists, scientists, and enthusiasts to enable effective collaboration between humans and AI. FathomVerse, a mobile game designed to inspire a new wave of ocean explorers, teaches casual gamers about ocean life while improving machine learning models and expanding annotated datasets (FathomNet). Of the three billion gamers worldwide, up to 70% say they care about the environment; FathomVerse taps into this engaged community with innovative gameplay and rich graphics that draw players into the captivating world of underwater imagery and cutting-edge ocean science. Here we will share our process of designing FathomVerse, discuss early successes from the v1 launch on May 1, 2024, and highlight some areas of future focus. In less than two weeks after v1 launch, 5k players from 90 different countries generated >2M annotations that are currently being used to generate consensus labels. Through FathomVerse, we hope to activate audiences in high school and up, providing social engagement and workforce education, with the goal of increasing public awareness and inspiring empathy for ocean life. Speaker Biography Dr. Kakani Katija is a Principal Engineer at the Monterey Bay Aquarium Research Institute and has a PhD in Bioengineering from the California Institute of Technology. As lead of the Bioinspiration Lab , Kakani and her group investigates ways that imaging and broad community engagement can enable observations of ocean life. By developing novel imaging and illumination tools (e.g., DeepPIV , EyeRIS ), automating the processing of visual data using artificial intelligence ( FathomNet ), building large-scale community science contributions through mobile gaming ( FathomVerse ), and integrating next-generation algorithms ( ML-Tracking , DeepSTARia ) on robotic vehicles (e.g. Mesobot , ROVs, and AUVs ) to consistently and persistently observe ocean life, her group’s efforts will increase access to biology and related phenomena in the deep sea. She has received generous funding support from the Packard Foundation, National Geographic Society, NSF, NOAA, Schmidt Ocean Institute, Dalio Philanthropies, Schmidt Marine Technology Partners, and the Moore Foundation. title: AAAI 2025 Workshop: Anomaly Detection in Scientific Domains
text: AAAI 2025 Workshop: Anomaly Detection in Scientific Domains Event dates Tue, Mar 4 2025, 9am - 6pm Event details Description Scientific discovery often involves the observation of an inconsistency among “normal” patterns within data. Recognizing something different, incongruous with the data, is what we call anomaly detection, which differs from other tasks since we do not know what exactly to look for—just to look for something different. This workshop aims to nurture the community of researchers at the intersection of machine learning and various scientific domains. Additionally, we will hold the award ceremony for the 1st HDR Interdisciplinary Machine Learning Challenge ( nsfhdr.org/mlchallenge ). This anomaly detection competition comprises one challenge in each of biology, physics, and climate science, with a combined challenge across domains. Integration of FAIR and Reproducible science is a critical element. Format Our 1-day workshop will include keynote/invited talks, contributed paper presentations, a poster session, a panel discussion, and presentations by the challenge winners. Attendance The intended audience includes AI/ML/data science researchers working on topics such as anomaly or out-of-distribution detection, open world recognition, scientific discovery, and FAIR dataset and reproducible workflows, looking for novel interdisciplinary research problems; domain scientists working on data-driven scientific discoveries. Call for Paper Submission Topics We encourage participation from researchers in a broad range of topics that explore AI/ML techniques to detect novel patterns and anomalies within data and promote scientific discovery. Examples of research questions include (but are not limited to): How can we automate the discovery of new scientific phenomena? How can we embed a notion of uncertainty within AI/ML to quantify the significance of a discovery? How do we ensure FAIR reproducibility of these discoveries? What interpretable AI/ML approaches can lead to direct explanations of these discoveries? Key Dates Paper Submission Deadline: December 6, 2024. 11:59 PM AOE Acceptance/Rejection Decision: December 16, 2024 Early Registration Deadline: December 19, 2024. 11:59 PM AOE Camera-Ready Deadline: February 6, 2025, 11:59 PM AOE Poster Deadline: February 20, 2025, 11:59 PM AOE Workshop Date: March 4, 2025 We offer an extended deadline for submissions with the same Camera-Ready and Poster Deadlines, but keep in mind that these are after the AAAI Early Registration Deadline has passed. Paper Submission Deadline: December 31, 2024. 11:59 PM AOE Acceptance/Rejection Decision: January 15, 2024 Submission Requirements We are accepting extended abstract submissions for position, review, or research results (up to 2 pages, excluding references). Shorter versions (up to 6 pages, excluding references) of articles in submission or accepted at other venues (or presented after Oct. 1, 2024) are acceptable as long as they do not violate the dual-submission policy of the other venue. We allow the addition of an appendix (no page limit) following references. All submissions will undergo peer review (double-blind). Submissions should follow the AAAI template format (two-column, camera-ready style; AAAI Author Kit ) and submitted via CMT. The accepted paper will NOT be archived in AAAI proceedings. This allows the authors to extend their work afterward and submit it to a conference or journal. Submit Your Work Today! title: Imageomics Workshop at AAAI 2025
text: Imageomics Workshop at AAAI 2025 Event dates Mon, Mar 3 2025, 9am - 5pm Location Philadelphia , PA United States Event link Workshop Details Event details Overview Imageomics is an emerging field of science that uses images, ranging from microscopic images of single-cell species to videos of charismatic megafauna such as giraffes and zebras, as the source of automatically extracted biological information, specifically traits, in order to gain insights into the evolution of function of living organisms. A central goal of Imageomics is to make traits computable from images, including the morphology, physiology, behavior, and genetic make-up of organisms, by grounding AI models in existing scientific knowledge so that they produce generalizable and biologically meaningful explanations of their predictions. Spearheaded by our prior research and community building efforts in this area as part of the NSF HDR Imageomics Institute , Imageomics is ripe with opportunities to form foundational bridges between AI and biological sciences by enabling computers to see what biologists cannot see while addressing key challenges in AI, creating a virtuous cycle between the two fields. The goal of this workshop is to nurture the community of researchers working at the intersection of AI and biology and shape the vision of the nascent yet rapidly growing field of Imageomics. Topics We encourage participation on a broad range of topics that explore AI/ML techniques to understand characteristic patterns of organisms from image or video data. Examples of research questions include (but are not limited to): What are the types and characteristics of knowledge and data in biology that can be integrated into AI methodologies, and what are the mechanisms for this integration? How best can new knowledge exposed by ML be translated back into the knowledge corpus of biology? How best can we inform and catalyze a community of practice to utilize and build upon Imageomics to address grand scientific and societal challenges? How can foundation models in vision and language impact biology or benefit from biological knowledge? Attendance We welcome participation from anyone interested in learning about the field of Imageomics, including (a) biologists working on problems with image data and biological knowledge available such as phylogenies, taxonomic groupings, ontologies, or evolutionary models, and (b) AI researchers working on topics such as explainability, generalizability, inductive bias, open world and fine-grained recognition, foundation models, and novelty detection, who are looking for novel interdisciplinary research problems. Symposium Key Dates: Good news! The deadline to submit papers for the Imageomics Workshop at AAAI has been extended. There are now two opportunities to submit your work for consideration. The first round aligns with AAAI’s early registration deadline of December 19, 2024, but we will also accept submissions through January 3, 2025. title: Seminar: Explore the PANGEA Project with Elsa Ordway
text: Seminar: Explore the PANGEA Project with Elsa Ordway Event dates Fri, Mar 7 2025, 11am - 12pm Event details Explore the PANGEA Project with Elsa Ordway Join us for a joint Imageomics Institute and ABC Global Climate Center seminar featuring Dr. Elsa Ordway, Professor at UCLA and Principal Investigator of the PANGEA Project. What: Special seminar on the PANGEA Project, NASA's latest decadal terrestrial ecology campaign. When: March 7, 11 a.m. Learn how PANGEA leverages field data and cutting-edge remote sensing technologies to examine the impacts of climate and land-use changes on tropical forests across continents. The project builds on the legacy of successful NASA campaigns like ABoVE and LBA-ECO. Register here: go.osu.edu/Elsa-Ordway Bio: Elsa Ordway is Co-Director of both the Center for Tropical Research and the Congo Basin Institute. She joined UCLA as an Assistant Professor in the Department of Ecology and Evolutionary Biology in 2021. She joined the Institute of the Environment and Sustainability as Affiliated Faculty in 2022. Before that, she was a Harvard University Center for the Environment Postdoctoral Fellow. Elsa earned a PhD in Earth System Science from Stanford University in 2018 and a Master’s in Conservation Biology from Columbia University in 2013 and has published articles on a range of issues relating to forest ecosystems and global change since then. Elsa’s research group examines social-ecological systems in forested regions in the context of two globally pressing challenges: climate change and increasing demands for land to accommodate food, fuel, and fiber production for ten billion people. How we choose to address these challenges will have far-reaching impacts on ecological processes, biodiversity, and society. Combining remote sensing, field observations, models, and socioeconomic analyses, her research group integrates theory and methods from ecology, earth science, economics, and land system science to gain new insight into pattern and process across scales in forests. They are primarily working in forested systems in the tropics and California. They also work closely with collaborators at the Congo Basin Institute and the NASA Jet Propulsion Laboratory Carbon Cycle & Ecosystems group. For more about PANGEA and its groundbreaking science, visit tropicalforestscoping.com/about . text: Seminar: Fishing for Data – Three Vignettes on Image-Based Research in Fish Event dates Mon, Apr 14 2025, 4 - 5pm Event details Fishing for Data with Becky Fuller Join us for a seminar hosted by the Imageomics Institute featuring Dr. Becky Fuller , Professor at the University of Illinois, Urbana-Champaign and head of the Department of Evolution, Ecology, and Behavior. Dr. Fuller will present three research vignettes that illustrate the use of image data to study: The evolution of coloration in relation to lighting environments and visual systems The evolution of fin size and shape as it relates to sex and mating systems Speciation and the diagnosis of hybrids in nature She will also discuss a new project using AI techniques to detect species and hybrids in collaboration with the Imageomics Group. Since 2005, she has been a faculty member at the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign , where she is now a full professor and head of the Department of Evolution, Ecology, and Behavior. title: Wild Data: Showcasing AI for Ecology and the Field of Imageomics
text: Wild Data: Showcasing AI for Ecology and the Field of Imageomics Event dates Thu, Apr 17 2025, 3 - 5:30pm Registration Register here to attend Event details Join us for a public showcase of student research from the year-long AI & Ecology course ! Students will present the results of their projects which use AI methods to investigate ecological questions, built on data collected during a January field course in Hawaii and connected to ongoing conservation efforts on the island. text: NSF HDR Community Conference 2025 Event dates Tue, Sep 16 - Fri, Sep 19 2025, All day Location Columbus , OH 43210 United States Event link NSF HDR Home Event details NSF HDR Ecosystem Conference 2025 September 16–19, 2025 • Columbus, OH and hosted by the Imageomics Institute. What’s the Conference About? The NSF Harnessing the Data Revolution (HDR) Ecosystem Conference is the premier national gathering of the HDR network—an integrated fabric of institutes, TRIPODS, Data Science Corps, and more—that are accelerating data-driven discovery across science and engineering. This year marks a pivotal convergence in Columbus, uniting researchers, practitioners, and students to share breakthroughs and chart a bold, data-rich future. Location & Date 📅 September 16–19, 2025 Starts: Tuesday at 6:00 PM Ends: Friday at 1:30 PM 🗺️ Location: Marriott Columbus OSU in Columbus, Ohio What’s on the Agenda This year's conference theme, Data to Discovery: The Future of AI-Enabled Science, is designed to propel the HDR Ecosystem into the next phase of scientific discovery. This year's sessions are centered around four subthemes: Theme 1: The Shape of AI for Science This theme explores how AI is transforming scientific discovery—enabling researchers to ask bigger, cross-scale questions and uncover fundamental insights about the natural world, from molecules to ecosystems to the entire planet. Through featured speakers, HDR project talks, and translational sessions, we’ll highlight frontier opportunities in AI-driven science. Theme 2: From Bits to Semantics This theme focuses on how we move from raw data to meaningful understanding. It examines how we ask scientific questions, represent knowledge, connect diverse datasets, and build interpretable, structured AI systems. Through featured speakers and breakout sessions, we’ll explore how to make sense of heterogeneous data and create AI that is not only powerful but also understandable and usable across disciplines. Topics for exploration include common cyberinfrastructure challenges, essential components ("parts list"), and exploring collaborative approaches to data infrastructure and sustainability. Theme 4: Education and Workforce Development This theme focuses on cultivating AI and data literacy skills across the educational spectrum—from K–12 to university to professional upskilling. Emphasis will be placed on developing innovative approaches to preparing the future AI-enabled workforce. The NextGen Forum will offer students, postdocs, and early career researchers a space for open discussion and collaboration as they shape the next generation of AI-driven science. From AI‑powered biodiversity and climate science to advanced cyberinfrastructure and workforce development, HDR projects exemplify convergent science addressing societal grand challenges. Community synergy is nourished. Building on the momentum of the 2022–2024 conferences, this year focuses on deepening collaborations, showcasing accomplishments, and scaling research across domains. title: Seminar: BioCLIP 2 and BioCAP- Extending Species Classification to Rich Ecological Understanding
text: Seminar: BioCLIP 2 and BioCAP- Extending Species Classification to Rich Ecological Understanding Event dates Mon, Feb 9 2026, 4 - 5pm Event link Register for Zoom Meeting Event details Join us for our next seminar on February 9th at 4pm EST where Imageomics Postdoctoral Researcher, Dr. Jianyang Gu will discuss BioCLIP2 and BioCAP and how these tools can advance ecological research. Abstract: Foundation models trained at scale can move beyond narrow recognition tasks and begin to encode higher-level structure about the world. In this talk, I will introduce BioCLIP 2, a large-scale vision-language model trained on 214M organismal images. The scaling leads to strong species classification performance, and more importantly, enables emergent ecological representations. Across benchmarks and case studies, I will highlight how the model supports practical workflows such as habitat classification and agricultural disease detection. I will then present BioCAP, a caption-augmented extension that enriches BioCLIP-style training with natural-language descriptions, improving the model’s ability to connect visual evidence with attributes, context, and broader ecological concepts. I will conclude with open challenges and opportunities on top of ecologically meaningful BioCLIP embeddings for the Imageomics community. Speaker Bio: Jianyang Gu is a Postdoctoral Researcher at The Ohio State University. He works on machine learning, computer vision, multimodal understanding, and their applications in scientific discovery. He is particularly interested in enriching or condensing data to understand the contribution of each data point to machine learning models. He has co-organized the Dataset Distillation workshop in CVPR 2024, the Anomaly Detection in Scientific Domains Workshop, and the Imageomics Workshop in AAAI 2025 and NeurIPS 2025. He served as an area chair for ICLR 2026 and ICML 2026, and a reviewer for multiple journals and conferences, including IEEE T-PAMI, NeurIPS, CVPR, ICCV, etc. Graphic from BioCLIP2. title: Seminar: Rethinking the Semantics of Biological Trait Recognition
text: Seminar: Rethinking the Semantics of Biological Trait Recognition Event dates Mon, Feb 23 2026, 4 - 5pm Event link Register for Zoom Meeting Event details Join us on Monday, February 23rd @4pm EST for the next Imageomics Seminar, Rethinking the Semantics of Biological Trait Recognition , featuring Sabina Leonelli. This talk builds on themes introduced in Dr. Leonelli’s plenary lecture at the Living Data Conference in October, bringing a timely and thought-provoking discussion on AI, human agency, and the future of biodiversity data ecosystems to our community. Abstract: This talk reflects on two challenges of biodiversity data sharing and analysis, and their interrelations. The first challenge is the integration of AI into data collection, management and analysis. The second challenge is the development of interoperable and sustainable data ecosystems at a moment of great digital fragility. I argue that these challenges can be confronted not by attempting to remove human agency and judgement from data analysis, but rather by articulating the role of human agency more clearly and placing it at the centre of data management, integration and mining activities. I exemplify this argument through examples from bio- ontologies and related forms of data semantics used to share biological trait data. Historically and conceptually, the study of biodiversity has been closely associated with the attempt to understand and preserve what Darwin aptly characterised as the “endless forms most beautiful and most wonderful”. Contemporary efforts to share phenomic data about organisms across different locations, and between high-resourced and low-resourced research environments, place in sharp relief the complexity and diversity of biological and environmental characteristics as well as of the methods used to generate and process data and the goals, skills and expectations of the stakeholders involved. I argue that the attempt to articulate semantic differences among plant varieties and methods of data collection, sharing and analysis is generating new ways to conceptualise and study organisms, including a reframing of the study of biodiversity. Speaker Bio: Sabina Leonelli is Chair of Philosophy and History of Science and Technology at the Technical University of Munich, where she directs the Ethical Data Initiative and the TUM Public Science Lab. Until 2024 she was Professor of Philosophy and History of Science, Director of the Centre for the Study of the Life Sciences (Egenis, 2013-2024) and lead on "Data Governance, Openness and Ethics" for the Institute for Data Science and Artificial Intelligence (IDSAI) at the University of Exeter, where she holds a Honorary Professorship. She serve as President of the International Society for History, Philosophy and Social Studies of Biology and European Climate Pact Ambassador; is the lead PI for the ERC project “A Philosophy of Open Science for Diverse Research Environments” (see website for several OA books and publications: www.opensciencestudies.eu ); and her book Data-Centric Biology won the Lakatos Award (2018) and Patrick Suppes Prize for Philosophy of Science (2022). title: Seminar: From Images to Insight: Cloud-Based Morphometrics and AI Classification of 3D Knockout Embryos
text: Seminar: From Images to Insight: Cloud-Based Morphometrics and AI Classification of 3D Knockout Embryos Event dates Mon, Mar 9 2026, 4 - 5pm Event link Register for Zoom Meeting Event details Please join us on Monday, March 9th @4pm EST for the next Imageomics Seminar, From Images to Insight: Cloud-Based Morphometrics and AI Classification of 3D Knockout Embryo s with Murat Maga ! Dr. Maga is a Professor in the Division of Craniofacial Medicine in the Department of Pediatrics at the University of Washington and a member of our Imageomics community. Abstract: Approximately 30% of genes are essential for mammalian development, yet we lack systematic tools to understand what happens when they malfunction. The International Mouse Phenotyping Consortium has generated thousands of high-resolution 3D scans of mouse embryos with specific gene knockouts—each representing a potential model for human birth defects. However, these extraordinary resources remain largely untapped because the severe malformations characteristic of these embryos defeat conventional image analysis methods, and modern artificial intelligence tools remain inaccessible to most biomedical researchers due to the complexity of managing the compute environments and workflows. I am going to present some of the tools we have been developing on how to tackle this challenge and make this data accessible and relevant for developmental genetics research. Speaker Bio: Dr. Murat Maga is a quantitative morphologist broadly interested in genetics and morphometrics of development in mammals. He integrates high-resolution 3D imaging and computational analysis to investigate complex form-and-function relationships. His foundational research deciphered the genetic architecture of the mouse craniofacial system and drove the development of automated, reproducible 3D landmarking pipelines utilizing diffeomorphic image registration and synthetic atlases. Currently, as a Principal Investigator at the Seattle Children’s Research Institute (SCRI), he studies the genetic basis of normal phenotypic variability and the factors that perturb that. title: Designing for Discovery: Shaping Imageomics Tools for Biologists
text: Designing for Discovery: Shaping Imageomics Tools for Biologists Event dates Thu, Apr 16 2026, 1 - 6pm Fri, Apr 17 2026, 8am - 1pm Location Columbus , OH 43210 United States Registration Registration: Tue, Mar 3 - Mon, Mar 30 2026, All day Event link Imageomics Conference Event details About the Event The Imageomics Institute is hosting a workshop as part of the Imageomics Conference , dedicated to bridging the gap between advanced computational tools and biological discovery. Within the field of imageomics, researchers have built a powerful suite of open-source tools; now, our mission is to evolve these into usable, community-wide resources. By partnering directly with biologists across all career stages, we aim to pressure-test existing workflows, uncover novel applications, and refine our messaging to ensure these tools are as intuitive as they are innovative. Motivation The first generation of Imageomics tools has proven successful in specialized applications, but we believe their true impact lies in their versatility. To realize this, we want to move beyond technical development and focus on usability and outreach . We are seeking the 'biological perspective' to help us translate complex toolsets into usable assets. By gathering community feedback, we aim to refine our communication and identify novel use cases that empower biologists—regardless of their computational background—to see their data in a new light. Scope This is a high-engagement, hands-on workshop designed for co-development. Rather than merely a traditional demonstration, this workshop functions as an active partnership where tool refinement and novel use cases emerge through real-time collaboration. Participants will explore a curated suite of Imageomics tools - ranging from taxonomic identification to trait segmentation and classification. We will specifically examine how these technologies can be used by domain scientists, for instance, to measure certain functional traits (i.e., morphological and behavioral) in ecology, as well as extract complex behavioral data from video. Who Should Participate We encourage participation from across the broader Imageomics Institute network, bringing together our biological and computational cohorts. This is a dedicated space for our ecologists and biologists, regardless of their technical expertise, to engage in a "deep dive" with our developers and data scientists. This internal partnership is vital to our iterative mission: leveraging our community’s diverse biological expertise to refine the Institute’s software tools and expand their research applications. Logistics 📅 Date & Location Thursday, April 16 (1:00 PM–5:00 PM) - Part 1: Open to all Imageomics Conference participants, this afternoon session will feature live demonstrations and tutorials. Friday, April 17 (8:00 AM–1:00 PM) - Part 2: This session will offer a deeper dive with a smaller group of conference participants and will include interactive, hands-on activities. Where: Energy Advancement and Innovation Center, The Ohio State University | Columbus, OH, USA 📝 How to Participate Because space for Part 2 of this community-centered workshop is limited, we ask all interested people to register for the Conference and select attendance at the 'Half-Day Workshop Add-on' during the registration process. This ensures we have an accurate headcount for the hands-on session. Imageomics Conference Registration ✈️ Travel Support We are committed to making this event accessible to our community across all institutional contexts. For those without access to NSF subaward-based travel funding marked for the Imageomics Institute All-Hands meeting (i.e., First Imageomics Conference), or who require additional financial support, limited travel assistance is available. Please indicate your specific funding needs when completing the I mageomics Conference Registration . Goals & Desired Outcomes This workshop seeks to: Empower biologists and ecologists with technical proficiency in the Imageomics toolkit. Co-develop novel workflows through real-time, iterative exercise of tool features. Identify high-impact research applications and unmet use cases for image-based data. Refine the Imageomics tool suite and value proposition to ensure clear, accessible communication for the broader life sciences community. title: Seminar - Beyond Species Identification: Pl@ntNet’s Large-Scale AI Pipeline for Downstream Biodiversity Inference
text: Seminar - Beyond Species Identification: Pl@ntNet’s Large-Scale AI Pipeline for Downstream Biodiversity Inference Event dates Thu, Apr 9 2026, 10 - 11am Event link Join Zoom Event details Please join us on Thursday April 9 @ 10am ET for an Imageomics Seminar, Beyond Species Identification: Pl@ntNet’s Large-Scale AI Pipeline for Downstream Biodiversity Inference , with Dr. Pierre Bonnet. Abstract: Pl@ntNet platform has evolved from a popular plant identification tool into a massive, AI-driven engine for computational ecology. This talk explores the core design and architecture of Pl@ntNet, detailing how millions of crowdsourced botanical images are processed to accurately identify species globally. Beyond taxonomic identification, we will examine how this rich data stream produces novel ecological insights through cutting-edge downstream applications. Highlights include GeoPl@ntNet's species distribution modeling based on high-resolution satellite and environmental data, as well as our diverse approaches to analyzing plant communities, focusing on the implementation of Large languages models (cf. Pl@ntBERT) or multi-scale tiling frameworks for complex plant image analysis. Finally, I will discuss the recent opening of the platform for automated plant disease identification, and explore the potential of Pl@ntNet's spatio-temporal data for conducting large-scale ecological studies. Speaker Bio: Pierre Bonnet is a biologist at CIRAD and co-lead of the Pl@ntNet citizen science platform. His research sits at the interface of ecology, biodiversity informatics, and machine learning, with a focus on designing and evaluating AI methods for plant identification and on translating large, heterogeneous biodiversity data streams into operational monitoring services. His work spans methodological contributions (from data curation and model evaluation to large-scale mapping workflows) and the deployment of end-user tools that enable practitioners to explore, validate, and use biodiversity indicators derived from major data infrastructures. He is the coordinator of the EU-funded GUARDEN project, and involved in the MAMBO EU project, dedicated to the development of new methods for large scale biodiversity monitoring and evidence-based decision-making. He also serves as a representative of Pl@ntNet within the World Flora Online consortium, supporting interoperability between citizen-science observations, taxonomic reference systems, and global flora initiatives. title: Seminar: Pixels are data: image analysis tools for known and unknown unknowns
text: Seminar: Pixels are data: image analysis tools for known and unknown unknowns Event dates Mon, Apr 20 2026, 4 - 5pm Event link Register for Zoom Meeting Event details Please join us Monday, April 20 @4pm EST on Zoom for the next Imageomics Seminar, Pixels are data: image analysis tools for known and unknown unknowns, with Dr. Beth Cimini . Abstract: In the era of the digital camera, pixels from microscopy images aren't just about what your eyes can see anymore- correctly captured and analyzed, they're an incredibly rich data source. In this talk, we'll discuss approaches to use this data to address both the things you know you want to find in your sample, and previously-unsuspected connections between samples. We'll also discuss tools and resources for making it easier and faster to analyze whatever samples you have. Speaker Bio: Dr. Beth Cimini is the Director of Bioimage Analysis at the Imaging Platform at the Broad Institute in Cambridge, MA. She obtained a PhD in Biochemistry and Molecular Biology with Dr. Elizabeth Blackburn at UCSF followed by postdoctoral and staff scientist roles with Dr. Anne Carpenter's lab at the Broad, leading a team collaborating with ~30 outside scientists per year on custom image analysis projects. The Cimini lab (est 2021) focuses on bioimage analysis tool creation (Piximi, Bilayers) and maintenance (CellProfiler), as well as on applying open source tools to novel biological problems. She created and directs the Platform's Postdoctoral Training Program in Bioimage Analysis, and also leads the Broad efforts on community engagement and technology development for the Center for Open Bioimage Analysis (COBA). She is a proud recipient of both the Association of Biomolecular Resource Facilities Alan Smith "Mentor of the Year" award as well as BioImaging North America's Michael W Davidson award for contributions in "Inclusion, Education, Mentorship, Standardization, and/or Advocacy". title: AI and Ecology Course: Module 0 Week 1 (Orientation: Administration and Introduction to Course Tools)

title: Seminar: A Generative Pretrained Transformer for Genomic Photosynthesis (GPTgp)
text: Seminar: A Generative Pretrained Transformer for Genomic Photosynthesis (GPTgp) Event dates Mon, Sep 21 2026, 4pm – 5pm Eastern Event details Lianhong Gu and Mengjun Shu of Oak Ridge National Laboratory present GPTgp, an AI foundation model project connecting genomic variation with photosynthetic traits. Overview This Department of Energy Genesis Mission pilot combines DNA language models with biological measurements to study photosynthesis across species. The team is developing reproducible training and evaluation workflows, with attention to explainability and uncertainty, to support research into how genetic differences affect photosynthetic systems. Speakers Lianhong Gu , a Distinguished Scientist in ORNL’s Environmental Sciences Division, leads GPTgp and studies photosynthesis through measurement, theory, and modeling. Mengjun Shu , an R&D Associate Staff Scientist in ORNL’s Biological Sciences Division and GPTgp co-investigator, studies the genetic basis of tree responses to environmental stress. Read the full abstract and speaker biographies on the original event page . Plant leaf with DNA strand and AI. title: Image Datapalooza 2023
text: Image Datapalooza 2023 Event dates Mon, Aug 14 2023, 8am - Thu, Aug 17 2023, 1pm Location The Ohio State University Pomerene Hall 1760 Neil Ave. Columbus , OH 43210 United States Event link View Call for Participation Event details The Imageomics Institute is hosting a 3.5-day workshop to address the scarcity of ML-ready image and video datasets focused on addressing scientific questions. The event will bring together an interdisciplinary group around a shared interest of using AI/ML to extract scientific knowledge from image and video data, including ML researchers, domain scientists, information scientists, tool developers, and data curators. Participants will work in small groups to collaboratively curate or develop FAIR datasets, best practices, tools, infrastructure, and other products targeting the motivating challenge. The by invitation only event will take place August 14-17 at The Ohio State University in Columbus, OH . title: Imageomics Seminar: Predicting multiple dimensions of plant diversity using airborne imagery and hierarchical models
text: Imageomics Seminar: Predicting multiple dimensions of plant diversity using airborne imagery and hierarchical models Event dates Mon, May 13 2024, 4 - 5pm Event link Register for Zoom Meeting Event details On May 13 the Imageomics Institute will welcome several researchers from the NSF Biology Integration Institute ASCEND . Dr. Jesús Pinto-Ledezma will give a presentation on his recent research. Predicting multiple dimensions of plant diversity using airborne imagery and hierarchical models Tracking biodiversity across biomes over time has emerged as an imperative in unified global efforts to manage our living planet for a sustainable future for humanity. We harness the National Ecological Observatory Network (NEON) to develop routines using airborne imaging spectroscopy to predict multiple dimensions of plant diversity at a continental scale across biomes in the US. Our findings indicate that diversity metrics based on spectral species (SS) from airborne spectroscopy data show strong and positive associations with ground-based species richness and other dimensions of plant diversity. In contrast, metrics based on distance matrices did not. Using a multi-level modeling framework, we find that spectral diversity consistently predicts analogous metrics of plant taxonomic, functional, and phylogenetic dimensions of biodiversity across biomes. The approach demonstrates promise for monitoring dimensions of plant diversity by integrating ground-based measures of biodiversity with imaging spectroscopy and advances capacity towards a Global Biodiversity Observing System. title: Imageomics Seminar: Shape is data and all data have shape: from leaf morphology to the shape of gene expression across flowering plants
text: Imageomics Seminar: Shape is data and all data have shape: from leaf morphology to the shape of gene expression across flowering plants Event dates Mon, May 6 2024, 4 - 5pm Event link Register for Zoom Meeting Event details Speaker Dan Chitwood Abstract Embedded in plant morphology is genetic, developmental, and environmental information. Quantifying the plant form and disentangling the effects of these factors potentially allows us to breed better crops, influence growth and yield, and anticipate how plants will respond to a changing climate. I will begin with an introduction to geometric morphometrics and its application to model the shapes of leaves, as a simple example of a closed contour. I will then talk about X-ray Computed Tomography (CT) reconstructions of plants, which although capture exquisite details down to micron resolution, present problems in how information is extracted from this type of data. Consequently, we have been using Topological Data Analysis (TDA) in collaboration with the lab of Dr. Elizabeth Munch, the motto of which is “shape is data, and all data have shape”. I will provide a qualitative introduction to TDA and its application to quantify diverse plant morphologies. I will also present participatory student research using TDA to visualize the structure of more abstract data types, including the structure of gene expression profiles across the flowering plants. Biography Dan Chitwood grew up in the Central Valley of California, where he worked for Ernest & Julio Gallo Winery and was introduced to viticulture and the study of leaf shape. He earned his undergraduate degree in Genetics from University of California, Davis and his PhD from Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory on Long Island, where he studied the morphogenetic contribution of small RNAs to leaf patterning. Afterwards he returned to U.C. Davis where he studied the quantitative genetic basis of leaf shape in tomato and wild relatives. His lab at Michigan State University continues to study shape but more abstractly, applying TDA approaches to complex datasets, including X-ray CT reconstructions, 2D images, and large, publicly available molecular datasets. He creates interdisciplinary, intercultural, and bilingual curricula that involve students in participatory research across the US and México.
